title: The Safehouse of Tashkent
premise: Juniper Kavanagh, a hostage negotiator whose one public failure haunts her career, takes a quiet off-the-books case: a defected analyst's family has vanished from a passenger manifest while the plane is still airborne. Following the erased trail to Tashkent, she uncovers a safehouse network that has been quietly sheltering witnesses against three governments—and discovers her own late father funded it, making her both heir and target. Hunted by an assassin who only kills people history has already erased, Juniper must smuggle a living witness and the flight's true passenger list past three intelligence services to a tribunal in Geneva. She survives by trading the one thing she swore never to give up: her anonymity, and with it the truth about her father's betrayal.
about_author: Rosalind Kavanagh is the pen name of a former crisis-line coordinator who spent a decade listening to people talk their way out of impossible rooms. She writes thrillers from a coastal cottage she refuses to geotag.

chapters.title: The Quiet Line
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. She talks a jumper off a Tashkent overpass via interpreter, then takes a private call from a fixer offering an unattributable case. The emotional beat is professional detachment cracking into curiosity—the first hook of a life she thought she'd left behind.

chapters.title: Manifest of Ghosts
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. She pulls the passenger list for Flight 442 and finds the analyst's family listed, then gone, mid-flight—no airline, no government will acknowledge the record existed. The beat is cold dread: someone can rewrite reality at 30,000 feet.

chapters.title: One Failure Still on the Board
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present-day Juniper. Her botched negotiation in Almaty, the hostage who died, and the anonymous letter that followed her for years. Emotional beat: shame weaponized—she realizes the letter's handwriting matches the fixer's.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wasn't Seated
chapters.summary: Juniper interviews the flight's purser in a Tashkent teahouse; he remembers a family who boarded and a seat that stayed warm. That night he's found drowned in a dry canal. The beat is guilt and acceleration—her questions are getting people erased.

chapters.title: Assassin of the Forgotten
chapters.summary: The assassin's POV, unnamed, methodical, killing only people already struck from records. He's ordered to leave Juniper alive 'for now.' The beat is chilling intimacy: he studies her file like scripture.

chapters.title: The Safehouse of Tashkent
chapters.summary: Juniper finds the safehouse behind a carpet merchant's storeroom: living witnesses, decades deep, kept by a network called the Ledger. Its dying custodian hands her a key and her father's name. The beat is vertigo—inheritance as ambush.

chapters.title: What My Father Bought
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, digging through her father's estate and finding payments, coded letters, and a photograph of the assassin as a boy the network once sheltered. The beat is grief curdling into anger at being made a custodian without consent.

chapters.title: Three Governments, One Lie
chapters.summary: A joint briefing scene: intelligence officers from three capitals agree, off-record, that Flight 442 never existed and that Juniper is now a problem. The beat is institutional menace—the machinery of erasure turning toward her.

chapters.title: The Witness in the Wall
chapters.summary: Inside the safehouse, Juniper meets Ilkhom, the flight's actual navigator, hidden for years, who can testify the plane landed at a black site. The beat is fragile hope—her first living proof.

chapters.title: Negotiation at Gunpoint
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The fixer reveals himself as her father's old partner and demands she surrender Ilkhom to buy her own exit. She negotiates a 72-hour window instead. The beat is her craft under existential pressure—talking with everything at stake.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Living
chapters.summary: The safehouse residents vote on whether to trust Juniper; an old woman who was erased in 1989 speaks for her. The beat is earned belonging—Juniper accepted by people whose survival depends on judgment.

chapters.title: The Assassin's Mercy
chapters.summary: The assassin's POV. He corners Juniper, recognizes her father's name, and lets her go with a warning: 'I only erase the forgotten. Make her remembered.' The beat is terrifying grace—the hunt reframed as a deadline.

chapters.title: Seventy-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Juniper plans the run to Geneva: forged documents, a rail route through three borders, Ilkhom sedated in a diplomatic car. The fixer's betrayal is implied. The beat is taut competence shadowed by dread.

chapters.title: Border of Salt
chapters.summary: The crossing goes wrong at a checkpoint; Juniper trades her father's ledger page to a corrupt colonel to pass. The beat is the price of survival made literal—she's spending her inheritance to save a stranger.

chapters.title: The Train That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: On the night train, Juniper discovers the fixer's man among the passengers and stages a silent confrontation in the dining car. The assassin intervenes—neutrally, for now. The beat is a three-way chess match in a moving box.

chapters.title: What the Fixer Wanted
chapters.summary: The fixer's POV. His motive: the Ledger names him, and he'll burn the network to stay clean, including Juniper. The beat is banal evil—erasure as self-preservation, not ideology.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Terminal
chapters.summary: At the Geneva rail terminal, the fixer's men take Ilkhom; Juniper, wounded, must choose between chasing the witness and broadcasting the flight records she's carried all along. The beat is sacrifice—she goes loud, ending her invisibility.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. She leaks the manifest to the tribunal and to every press desk simultaneously, making Ilkhom too famous to erase. The fixer's network begins to burn. The beat is catharsis through exposure—truth as a weapon of scale.

chapters.title: The Last Erasure
chapters.summary: The assassin's POV. Ordered to erase the fixer, he instead delivers him—alive—to the tribunal, honoring his one rule by refusing the final job. The beat is a killer choosing memory over obedience.

chapters.title: Tribunal of the Remembered
chapters.summary: Ilkhom testifies; three governments flinch in daylight. Juniper, publicly named and unmade as a ghost herself, watches her father's name enter the record. The beat is bittersweet vindication—truth won, innocence lost.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. She returns to Tashkent, reopens the safehouse under new custodians, and finds a final letter from her father: an apology, and the name of the next flight. The beat is acceptance—she keeps the debt rather than the money.

chapters.title: The Quiet Line, Again
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, mirrored opening. A new anonymous call offers a new erased case; she answers as the Ledger's keeper, the assassin listening on the line as her unlikely sentinel. The beat is resolve—the invisible now guard the forgotten.
